subject: physics
title: Circular motion
key_idea: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is always accelerating, because its direction keeps changing. The acceleration, and the resultant force that causes it, point to the centre of the circle.

blocks.text: This section covers how to measure an angle in radians and how fast an object turns round a circle.

items.meaning: The angle at the centre of a circle when the arc length equals the radius.
The angle, in radians, through which an object has turned about the centre.
The time for one complete revolution.
The number of complete revolutions per second.
The angle turned per unit time, in rad/s.

items: A full circle has an arc length of 2πr, so it is **2π radians**.
2π rad = 360°, so π rad = 180°.
To change degrees to radians, multiply by π / 180. To change radians to degrees, multiply by 180 / π.
A radian has no unit in calculations, but it is written as rad.
Every point on a spinning object has the same ω.
A point further from the centre has a larger r, so it has a larger v.
The speed v is constant but the velocity is not, because the direction keeps changing.
One radian is the angle when arc length equals radius; 2π rad = 360°.
ω = 2π / T = 2πf, and v = ωr.
Constant speed in a circle means changing velocity.

blocks.text: Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity. That change is an acceleration.

items: The velocity is along the tangent to the circle at every instant.
The change in velocity points towards the centre.
So the acceleration is towards the centre. It is called **centripetal acceleration**.
It changes the direction of the velocity but not the speed.

blocks.text: The two forms agree because v = ωr. Use v²/r when you know the speed, and ω²r when you know the angular speed or the period.

items: Centripetal acceleration points to the centre and is perpendicular to the velocity.
a = v² / r = ω²r.
It changes the direction of motion, not the speed.

blocks.text: Newton's second law says an acceleration needs a resultant force. For circular motion this is the centripetal force.

blocks.label: Centripetal force
where: F = resultant force towards the centre (N)

items: The force has constant size and is always perpendicular to the direction of motion.
A force perpendicular to the motion does no work, so the speed stays constant.
Centripetal force is not a new kind of force. It is the name for the resultant force towards the centre.
Something real provides it: tension in a string, friction on a tyre, gravity on a satellite, or the normal contact force.

diagram.alt: A slider showing how centripetal acceleration and force change with mass, speed and radius.

items: A resultant force towards the centre is needed to keep an object in a circle.
F = mv² / r = mω²r.
Doubling the speed quadruples the force needed.

checks.q: A car travels at a constant 20 m/s round a bend of radius 50 m. Explain why it is accelerating, and calculate the acceleration.
checks.a: Its direction, and so its velocity, is changing, so it accelerates. a = v² / r = 20² / 50 = 8.0 m/s², towards the centre of the bend.

checks.q: A wheel turns at 120 revolutions per minute. Calculate its angular speed in rad/s.
A 0.40 kg mass moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m at 3.0 rad/s. Calculate the centripetal force, and state what provides it if the mass is on a string.
checks.a: F = mω²r = 0.40 × 3.0² × 0.80 = 2.9 N. It is provided by the tension in the string.

items: Angular speed is written ω = v / r = 2πf.
The direction of angular velocity is not considered, so treat ω as a size only.
You use the formulae for centripetal acceleration but do not have to derive them.

blocks.text: You must be able to use vector diagrams to derive a = v² / r.

items.text: Draw the velocity vectors v₁ and v₂ at two points a small angle Δθ apart. They have the same length v.
Place them tail to tail. The change in velocity Δv joins their tips and points towards the centre.
For a small angle, Δv ≈ vΔθ.
a = Δv / Δt = v × Δθ / Δt = vω.
Using ω = v / r gives a = v² / r, and using v = ωr gives a = ω²r.

items: Use T = 2π / ω to link the period to the angular speed.
Convert between degrees and radians in any angular displacement.
Define the radian: the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.
A force of constant magnitude that is always perpendicular to the motion causes centripetal acceleration.
Centripetal acceleration produces circular motion with a constant angular speed.

extra.heading: Investigating circular motion with a whirling bung

blocks.text: A rubber bung on a string is whirled in a horizontal circle. The string passes through a tube, and weights hang from the lower end to give the tension.

items.text: Hang a known weight below the tube. Its weight W gives the tension, which is the centripetal force.
Whirl the bung so the marker on the string stays just below the tube. This keeps the radius constant.
Time 10 or more revolutions with a stopwatch and divide to find the period T.
Find v = 2πr / T, or ω = 2π / T, and compare F = mv² / r with the weight.
Change the weight, then the radius, one at a time to see how T changes.

items: Timing many revolutions reduces the effect of reaction time.
The string is not exactly horizontal, so the measured tension is slightly different from the true centripetal force.
